notes:
Here is a verse-by-verse commentary on 2 Kings 10, drawing on the traditional readings of trusted pastors and teachers, noting tradition-specific perspectives where available, and flagging what could not be found.

---

## 2 Kings 10 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary

### v. 1: *Now Ahab had seventy sons in Samaria. So Jehu wrote letters and sent them to Samaria to the officials of Jezreel, to the elders, and to the guardians of the sons of Ahab…*

**“Seventy sons”** is understood broadly as male descendants — grandsons and possibly great-grandsons of Ahab, not necessarily seventy immediate sons. Ahab had been dead about fourteen years and had a considerable harem (Ellicott). The number seventy may also be a round or conventional number signalling dynastic completeness rather than an exact head count (Precept Austin, citing ESV Study Bible). Gill notes these might not all be immediate sons but some grandsons, "as such are sometimes called in Scripture."

**Jehu’s letters** show his shrewd, calculating nature. He could not yet march on Samaria without first sounding out the loyalties of the city's leadership. Ellicott calls Jehu "crafty as well as fierce." Precept Austin notes that Jehu's letters represent "psychological warfare" — he forces the leaders to think, choose, and expose their allegiance *before any swords are drawn.*

**"Officials of Jezreel"**: Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary both argue that "Jezreel" is a textual corruption. The LXX reads "rulers of Samaria." The Pulpit Commentary suggests the original was "Israel" (ישׂראל), easily corrupted into "Jezreel" (יזרעאל). Jehu's letters were addressed to the leadership in Samaria, not Jezreel.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-10/
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-10-commentary
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/10.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-10.html

---

### vv. 2–3: *“When this letter arrives… select the best and most worthy son of your master, set him on his father’s throne, and fight for your master’s house.”*

Jehu's challenge is **mocking and ironic** — he dares them to do their worst. Ellicott detects "a tone of mocking irony in Jehu's challenge to the nobles of Samaria, who were probably as luxurious and cowardly now as in the days of Amos." By carefully enumerating their resources (chariots, horses, a fortified city, weaponry), Jehu implies that if they do *not* resist, it will not be for lack of military means but for lack of will. Precept Austin: "Jehu is not bullying the weak — he is confronting leaders who have every human resource necessary to oppose him." Gill calls his words a form of sarcasm and sneering.

Enduring Word (Guzik) notes that Jehu "challenged any partisans of the house of Omri to declare themselves and prepare to fight." Jehu is effectively conducting a test of loyalty: are you with Ahab's dynasty or with God's newly anointed king?

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-10/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/10.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-10.html

---

### v. 4: *But they were terrified and reasoned, “If two kings could not stand against him, how can we?”*

The leaders were "exceedingly afraid" — the Hebrew intensifies the fear (literally "they feared mightily, mightily"; Ellicott). They use a classic **lesser-to-greater** (qal-wahomer) argument: if the two kings (Joram of Israel and Ahaziah of Judah) could not stand before Jehu, how could mere city administrators hope to?

Precept Austin notes what is absent from their reasoning: "There is no mention of Yahweh. They see Jehu, but they do not see the God who anointed Jehu (2 Ki 9:6–7)." Their fear is pragmatic, not reverent.

- https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-10-commentary
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/10.htm

---

### v. 5: *So the palace administrator, the overseer of the city, the elders, and the guardians sent a message to Jehu: “We are your servants… Do whatever is good in your sight.”*

This is the **turning point** of the chapter. The entire leadership structure of Samaria capitulates without a fight. Precept Austin observes: "Jehu no longer faces internal resistance, and the capital city submits without a fight as Samaria's officials abandon Ahab's sons to save themselves." The irony is that "the very ones entrusted to protect the royal heirs would be commanded to take their royal heads."

Gill identifies "he that was over the house" as the prefect of the palace (major-domo) and "he that was over the city" as the civil governor. Ellicott notes that similar officials appear on Egyptian monuments.

- https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-10-commentary
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-10.html
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/10.htm

---

### v. 6: *Then Jehu wrote a second letter: “If you are on my side… bring the heads of your master’s sons to me at Jezreel by this time tomorrow.”*

Jehu now escalates. The leaders' words of loyalty must be proven by **the act of executing all seventy sons of Ahab**, making them irrevocably complicit in the coup. Precept Austin calls this "Jehu drops the hammer."

A noted textual ambiguity: the Hebrew word for "heads" (רֹאשׁ) can mean either **literal heads** or **leaders**. Peter Leithart (cited at Precept Austin) notes the ambiguity: Jehu's command could be read as "bring the leaders of your master's sons" — giving him deniability. The NET Bible note also flags this: "Jehu's command is intentionally vague… The city leaders interpret his words in the literal sense, but Jehu's command is so ambiguous he is able to deny complicity in the executions (see v. 9)."

- https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-10-commentary
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-10/

---

### v. 7: *And when the letter arrived, they took the sons of the king and slaughtered all seventy of them. They put their heads in baskets and sent them to Jehu at Jezreel.*

The guardians became executioners. Precept Austin: "These men were guardians, caretakers and civic leaders, most of whom had never lifted a sword against another person. Now, these men decapitate the 70 and send their heads to Jehu."

Trapp (cited in both Enduring Word and Precept Austin) notes a grim appropriateness: "This was suitable to Ahab's sin. He had sent for baskets of grapes out of Naboth's vineyard at Jezreel; and now the heads of his sons are brought thither in baskets."

The ESV Study Bible (cited at Precept Austin) observes that this kind of royal purge was "not at all uncommon in the ancient world" and cites the Aramaic Panammuwa Inscription (c. 733–727 BC) and Judges 9:5 (Abimelech killing seventy brothers) as parallels, suggesting seventy may be a round number or literary convention.

- https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-10-commentary
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-10/

---

### v. 8: *When the messenger arrived… Jehu ordered, “Pile them in two heaps at the entrance of the gate until morning.”*

The public display at the city gate — the place of legal decisions, market, and public assembly — was a standard ancient Near Eastern method of **deterring rebellion**. Precept Austin notes this was "a tactic also used by contemporary Neo-Assyrian kings" and references Assyrian reliefs depicting scribes counting piles of severed heads.

Gill suggests it was evening when the heads arrived; they were to be kept under guard overnight for maximum public exposure in the morning.

- https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-10-commentary
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-10.html

---

### v. 9: *The next morning, Jehu went out and stood before all the people and said, “You are innocent. It was I who conspired against my master and killed him. But who killed all these?”*

Jehu engages in a **calculated public-relations manoeuvre**. Poole (cited in Enduring Word) explains: "You are righteous in your own eyes, and you look upon me as a traitor… But if I am guilty, you are not innocent… for I have killed one, but you a great number." Jehu deflects blame onto the Samarian leaders while simultaneously implying that the massacre was divinely orchestrated.

Precept Austin: "By publicly confessing his own limited role while exposing the greater complicity of others, he neutralizes opposition, fulfills prophecy, and binds the nation to his reign through shared responsibility."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-10/
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-10-commentary

---

### v. 10: *“Know, then, that not a word the LORD has spoken against the house of Ahab will fail, for the LORD has done what He promised through His servant Elijah.”*

Jehu anchors the whole bloody episode in **the absolute reliability of God's prophetic word**. Precept Austin comments: "'Fall to the earth nothing of the word' is an idiomatic way of saying God's Word will not fail, come to nothing, or prove empty.… Divine delay does not signify divine denial." Jehu is referencing Elijah's prophecy in 1 Kings 21:21–24.

Ellicott renders it: "Jehovah, He hath done; or, and Jehovah it is who hath done" — emphasising that God Himself is the ultimate agent.

Yet Enduring Word notes the tension: "Jehu carried out God's will, but he went too far and executed more people than God intended" — a view voiced by Knapp and others.

- https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-10-commentary
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-10/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/10.htm

---

### v. 11: *So Jehu killed everyone in Jezreel who remained of the house of Ahab, as well as all his great men and close friends and priests, leaving him without a single survivor.*

This verse records the **systematic completion** of the judgment at Jezreel. Precept Austin notes it "is not a random slaughter, but a targeted purge" covering four categories: blood relatives, great men (high officials), close acquaintances, and priests. Gill adds that "his great men" were "ministers of state and counsellors, that advised him to, and abetted him in his idolatrous practices."

- https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-10-commentary
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-10.html

---

### v. 12: *Then Jehu set out toward Samaria. At Beth-eked of the Shepherds…*

"Beth-eked of the Shepherds" (literally "the binding-house of the shepherds") was probably a solitary building serving as a **shepherds' meeting-place** along the route from Jezreel to Samaria. Ellicott notes the root meaning: shepherds bound their sheep there for shearing. Eusebius (cited in Ellicott) mentions a village called Beithakad about fifteen Roman miles from Legio (Lejjûn).

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/10.htm

---

### vv. 13–14: *Jehu met some relatives of Ahaziah king of Judah… “Take them alive.” So his men took them alive, then slaughtered them at the well of Beth-eked — forty-two men.*

These were **kinsmen** of Ahaziah, not his literal brothers, since his brothers had already been killed by Arabs during Jehoram's lifetime (2 Chronicles 21:17; 22:1). They were travelling to visit the royal family in Jezreel, unaware of the coup. They mention "the queen mother" (Jezebel), which sealed their fate since it identified them as connected to the house of Ahab through Ahaziah's mother Athaliah (daughter of Ahab and Jezebel).

Enduring Word notes this is "to the great misfortune of these men." Some commentators, like Knapp (cited in Enduring Word), believe that "the sword of judgment, so far as the expressed purpose of Jehovah was concerned, should have been confined to the house of Ahab. But a reckless and ambitious hand was wielding it, and it devoured beyond the allotted limits."

**Tradition note**: This is one of the verses where commentators differ on whether Jehu exceeded his divine commission. The more cautious view (Gill, Ellicott, Matthew Henry) sees the execution of Ahaziah's relatives as legitimate since they were connected to the house of Ahab and idolatrous. Others (Knapp, some modern evangelical commentators) see it as Jehu going too far for political expediency.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-10/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/10.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-10.html

---

### vv. 15–16: *Jehu… found Jehonadab son of Rechab… “Is your heart as true to mine as my heart is to yours?”… “Come with me and see my zeal for the LORD!”*

**Jehonadab (Jonadab) son of Rechab** was the founder of the Rechabites, a reform movement that lived an austere, nomadic life in protest against the materialism and religious compromise in Israel (Jeremiah 35). Enduring Word notes they were "separatists to the core and strong patriots." According to Josephus (cited in Enduring Word), Jehu and Jehonadab were long-standing friends who both detested the luxurious lifestyle of the royal family.

Jehu's question about Jehonadab's heart and the handshake likely served a **political purpose**: by taking this revered religious leader into his chariot, Jehu gained legitimacy. Clarke (cited in Enduring Word): "Jehonadab was doubtless a very honourable man in Israel; and by carrying him about with him in his chariot, Jehu endeavoured to acquire the public esteem."

**"See my zeal for the LORD"** is a pivotal statement. On one hand, it reflects genuine energetic obedience; on the other, it reveals pride. Morgan (cited in Enduring Word): "His words to Jehonadab, 'Come with me, and see my zeal for Jehovah,' are in themselves a revelation of a proud spirit." Knapp adds: "His ostentatious display of his reforming zeal revealed how little he had God's glory in mind."

**John Piper (Reformed Baptist)** at Desiring God comments on this verse: "Jehu is a tragic figure… What a tragedy. God actually commended Jehu that he had 'done well.'… But there were two problems. Jehu still loved idols, if not Baal. And Jehu did not obey God with all his heart." Piper adds, "It is possible to have a kind of zeal for God that loves the external forms of Christianity but does not love God."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-10/
- https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/zeal-for-god-gone-wrong

---

### v. 17: *When Jehu came to Samaria, he struck down everyone belonging to Ahab who remained there, until he had destroyed them, according to the word that the LORD had spoken to Elijah.*

This completes the **extermination of Ahab's house** in Samaria, mirroring what was done at Jezreel (v. 11). The refrain "according to the word of the LORD… to Elijah" underscores the author's theological interpretation: these bloody events are divine judgment, not merely political violence.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-10.html

---

### v. 18: *Then Jehu brought all the people together and said, “Ahab served Baal a little, but Jehu will serve him a lot.”*

Jehu's statement is **deliberately deceptive**. He feigns devotion to Baal to lure all Baal-worshippers into a trap. Enduring Word: "Jehu feigned devotion to Baal to lure the priests and worshippers of Baal into a trap."

**Tradition differences on deception (vv. 18–19)**:

- **Gill (Reformed Baptist)** is cautious: "in which he is not to be justified, however good his intention was; for evil is not to be done that good may come."
- **The Church Pulpit Commentary (Anglican)** does not condemn Jehu's deception outright but sees in his zeal a mixture of good and evil: "Jehu's zeal burnt brightly… as long as it was fanned by the excitement of self-interest."
- **Enduring Word (Pentecostal/Charismatic)** notes the deception neutrally, focusing on the result.
- **Matthew Henry** (Reformed) sees the deception as part of Jehu's "subtilty" and is also cautious about justifying it.

The Catholic view could not be retrieved; a search for Haydock or newadvent.org material was unavailable.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-10/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-10.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cpc/2-kings-10.html (Church Pulpit Commentary, from search excerpts)

---

### v. 19: *“Now, therefore, summon to me all the prophets of Baal… See that no one is missing, for I have a great sacrifice for Baal.” But Jehu was acting deceptively in order to destroy the servants of Baal.*

The term translated "deceptively" (or "in subtilty," KJV) is the Hebrew word *'oqbāh*, which occurs only here. Ellicott notes it is related to the name Jacob ("supplanter"), from Genesis 25:26. The LXX renders it literally "in heeling" — i.e., tripping up, striking with the heel. Jarchi and Ben Gersom (cited in Gill) translate it "in deceit."

Ellicott compares this convocation to Elijah's similar gathering of Baal's prophets in 1 Kings 18:19ff. Jehu threatens death for anyone who fails to attend, which ensures **total attendance**.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/10.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-10.html

---

### v. 20: *And Jehu commanded, “Proclaim a solemn assembly for Baal.” So they announced it.*

A "solemn assembly" (*‘aṣārâ*) was a religious gathering where ordinary work was suspended — akin to a holy convocation. Ellicott notes that participants would have to "sanctify" or purify themselves. This added to the solemnity and ensured maximum participation.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/10.htm

---

### v. 21: *Then Jehu sent word throughout Israel, and all the servants of Baal came… They entered the temple of Baal, and it was filled from end to end.*

The temple of Baal in Samaria, built by Ahab (1 Kings 16:32), was **packed to capacity**. The Hebrew idiom "from end to end" is literally "mouth to mouth" — the building was brimful like a vessel filled right to its rim (Ellicott). Gill notes that the number of Baal worshippers may already have been reduced by the ministries of Elijah and Elisha, and by Joram's earlier removal of Baal's image.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/10.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-10.html

---

### v. 22: *And Jehu said to the keeper of the wardrobe, “Bring out garments for all the servants of Baal.”*

The distinctive **vestments** served two purposes: they added solemnity (the worshippers would think) and they **marked out every Baal-worshipper** so that none could hide or escape among civilians (the real intent). The word for "vestry" (*meltāhāh*) occurs only here in the Old Testament. Ellicott discusses possible cognates in Ethiopic meaning "linen robe."

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/10.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-10.html

---

### v. 23: *Next, Jehu and Jehonadab son of Rechab entered the temple of Baal, and Jehu said… “Look around to see that there are no servants of the LORD here among you.”*

Jehu's precaution to exclude worshippers of Yahweh would have appeared to the Baal-devotees as **reverence for Baal** — a dread lest some profane person be present in his sanctuary (Ellicott). In reality, Jehu wanted to avoid killing any true worshippers of the LORD who might be present out of curiosity.

Gill notes that Jehu himself may have considered the golden-calf worshippers as "servants of the LORD" — which, though false worship, he did not view as idolatry in the same sense as Baal-worship.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/10.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-10.html

---

### vv. 24–25: *And they went in to offer sacrifices… Now Jehu had stationed eighty men outside… “Go in and kill them. Do not let anyone out.”*

Jehu's eighty guardsmen surrounded the temple. The timing was chosen: **as soon as the chief priest had finished offering the burnt offering**, when all the worshippers were absorbed in the ritual (Ellicott). The guards "put them to the sword, threw the bodies out, and went into the inner room of the temple of Baal."

The Syriac version (cited by Ellicott) reads "when *they* [the Baal priests] had made an end" rather than Jehu personally offering — suggesting Jehu did not act as a sacrificing priest but let the Baal priests perform their own rites before the slaughter.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/10.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-10/

---

### vv. 26–27: *They brought out the sacred pillar of the temple of Baal and burned it. They also demolished the sacred pillar of Baal. Then they tore down the temple of Baal and made it into a latrine.*

The **total desecration** of the site was deliberate. Burning the sacred pillars (*maṣṣēbôt*), demolishing the temple, and turning it into a latrine (literally a "place for human excrement," as Clarke noted) was the ultimate degradation. Enduring Word: "Nothing could be more degrading than this."

Gill: "a fit place for dunghill gods to be thrown into, and an idol temple to be turned into."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-10/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-10.html

---

### v. 28: *Thus Jehu eradicated Baal from Israel.*

This is a genuine achievement, unique among the kings of the northern kingdom. Enduring Word: "He worked to completely eliminate the worship of Baal from Israel, making him a unique king among the other rulers of the Northern Kingdom." No other king of Israel fought against idolatry as aggressively as Jehu.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-10/

---

### v. 29: *But he did not turn away from the sins that Jeroboam son of Nebat had caused Israel to commit — the worship of the golden calves at Bethel and Dan.*

This is the **great flaw**. Jehu eradicated Baal-worship but retained the state-sponsored calf-worship established by Jeroboam I. Enduring Word explains the political calculus: "He knew that Israel had to come back to the true God, but he was unconcerned about how they did it. For Jehu, it was just as good to worship Yahweh at the temple of the golden calves at Dan or Bethel, and it was better for Israel if they did it at those places rather than at Jerusalem."

Gill adds: "partly because he might not think it idolatry, because God was worshipped in them… but chiefly lest the kingdom of Israel should return to the house of David, the worship of the calves being a piece of state policy, to keep them from going to Jerusalem to worship."

**MacLaren (Expositor's Bible)** comments: "Obedience has to be 'all in all, or not at all.' We may not 'compound for sins we are inclined to, by' zeal against those 'we have no mind to.'… Putting away Baal is of little use if we keep the calves at Dan and Beth-el."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-10/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-10.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mac/2-kings-10.html

---

### v. 30: *Nevertheless, the LORD said to Jehu, “Because you have done well in carrying out what is right in My sight… four generations of your sons will sit on the throne of Israel.”*

God **commends and rewards** Jehu's partial obedience. His dynasty would be the longest in the northern kingdom — Jehoahaz, Jehoash, Jeroboam II, and Zechariah (four generations). The Jews traditionally supposed this word came through the prophet Jonah son of Amittai (Gill).

Yet this verse must be read alongside **Hosea 1:4**, which pronounces judgment on the house of Jehu for "the bloodshed of Jezreel." Enduring Word explains the tension: both texts are true — Jehu was both good and bad. Three explanations are offered: (1) Jehu went too far and killed more than God intended, (2) he did God's will with wrong motives (pride, personal ambition), (3) his obedience was partial.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-10/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-10.html

---

### v. 31: *Yet Jehu was not careful to follow the instruction of the LORD, the God of Israel, with all his heart. He did not turn away from the sins that Jeroboam had caused Israel to commit.*

This is the **biblical verdict** on Jehu. Despite his zeal, he lacked a transformed heart. **Spurgeon (Reformed Baptist)**, in a sermon on this verse (cited in Enduring Word and the Church Pulpit Commentary), said: "Jehu did obey God up to a certain point. It happened to be a profitable thing to him to exterminate the old royal house of Ahab… but anything beyond that did not pay, and therefore Jehu did not touch it." Spurgeon also said: "Hating one sin he loved another, and thus proved that the fear of the Most High did not reign in his breast. He was merely a hired servant, and received the throne as his wages, but a child of God he never was."

**Morgan** (cited in Enduring Word): "How terrible a warning is the story of this man — that it is possible to be an instrument in the hand of God and yet never be in fellowship with Him."

**John Piper (Reformed Baptist)** at Desiring God: "Jehu was not careful to walk in the law of the Lord, the God of Israel, with all his heart.… It is possible… to have a kind of zeal for God today that loves the external forms of Christianity but does not love God."

**The Church Pulpit Commentary** (Anglican) asks: "Was Jehu, then, a hypocrite?… It is because there is so great a mixture of good and evil in his deeds, because there is so much in his character that deserves to be imitated while there is also, at the same time, a deadly flaw in it which mars its beauty, that his history is worthy of particular study."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-10/
- https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/zeal-for-god-gone-wrong
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cpc/2-kings-10.html

---

### vv. 32–33: *In those days the LORD began to reduce the size of Israel. Hazael defeated the Israelites throughout their territory from the Jordan eastward…*

The territorial losses are portrayed as **direct divine discipline**. Enduring Word: "This was the work of the LORD. These neighboring rulers and their kingdoms were prompted and made successful by God." The land east of the Jordan — Gilead, Bashan, and the territories of Gad, Reuben, and Manasseh — had been held by Israel for over 600 years since the conquest under Joshua. Now it was all lost to Hazael of Syria.

This fulfills the prophetic word in 1 Kings 19:17, where God told Elijah that Hazael would be one instrument of judgment.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-10/

---

### vv. 34–36: *As for the rest of the acts of Jehu… are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?… Jehu rested with his fathers… his son Jehoahaz reigned in his place. So the duration of Jehu's reign over Israel in Samaria was twenty-eight years.*

The standard **regnal formula** closes the account. Twenty-eight years was a long reign — the longest of any king of the northern kingdom — yet "notable only at its beginning," as Enduring Word observes. Clarke (cited in Enduring Word) remarks: "We have no chronicles in which there is any thing further spoken of this bad man. His reign was long, twenty-eight years; and yet we know nothing of it but the commencement."

Knapp (cited in Enduring Word) summarises: "The great lesson to be drawn from this remarkable man's life is that of being constantly on guard, as servants of God, lest we be found doing His work… in a spirit of unbrokenness and without due exercise of heart and conscience."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-10/

---

## Summary of Tradition-Specific Perspectives

| Issue | View | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Jehu's deception (vv. 18–19) | Cautious — "evil is not to be done that good may come" | Gill (Reformed Baptist) |
| Jehu's deception (vv. 18–19) | Described neutrally; focus on result | Enduring Word (Pentecostal/Charismatic) |
| Jehu's zeal (v. 16) | Proud, ostentatious, self-promoting | Morgan, Knapp (cited in Enduring Word); MacLaren (Expositor's) |
| Jehu's heart (v. 31) | "A child of God he never was" — unregenerate servant | Spurgeon (Reformed Baptist) |
| Jehu's heart (v. 31) | Possible to serve God externally without loving Him | Piper (Reformed Baptist, Desiring God) |
| Jehu's mixed character (v. 31) | Mixture of good and evil, not outright hypocrisy | Church Pulpit Commentary (Anglican) |
| Jehu exceeding his commission (vv. 13–14) | "The sword devoured beyond the allotted limits" | Knapp (cited in Enduring Word) |
